Present Perfect Continuous vs Present Perfect + Since and For for Duration

You use both the Present Perfect Continuous and the Present Perfect to talk about finished actions and unfinished actions.

The Present Perfect tense is used to talk about an action that started in the past and continues up to the present. You often include the words since and for with the Present Perfect. For indicates the period of time the action has been happening and since indicates the point in time when the action began.
You often use the Present Perfect tense when explaining how much or how many.

Example:
I've not e-mailed my friend for a long time.
Steve has drunk two cups of coffee already!
You can also use the Present Perfect Continuous to talk about an action that started in the past and continues up to the present.
You use the Present Perfect Continuous tense to emphasize the passage of time (how long an action has been happening up to the present).

Example:
She's been working on her online profile for a long time.
Julie has been drinking the same coffee since early this morning!
I have been fascinated by different ideas, religions and cultures since I was a child.
I have been single for a few years now.
I have been working since my late teens.

Phrasal verbs consist of a verb and one or more prepositions. They are often used, especially in informal spoken English. The meaning of phrasal verbs is often completely different from the meaning of the verb alone.
Phrasal verbs can either be separable or inseparable.
Separable phrasal verbs consist of two parts. They always require an object.
The object of a phrasal verb can go either between the verb and the preposition or after the preposition.

Examples:
I looked up the word in the dictionary.
I looked the word up in the dictionary.

If the object of the sentence is a pronoun, it must go between the two parts of the phrasal verb.
Example:
I looked it up in the dictionary.
Some phrasal verbs are inseparable. With inseparable phrasal verbs, the preposition or adverb must be placed directly after the verb.

Examples:
  • settle down = get married
    I'm looking for the right person to settle down with.
  • eat out = eat at a restaurant
    I love going to see live music and eating out at interesting restaurants.
  • break up = end a relationship
    However, I'd rather be a slightly lonely singleton than be with just anyone to be part of a couple only to quickly break up.

images.text:
This profile looks interesting ...

It's really difficult to talk about yourself but I will give it a try.
My close friends often tell me that I am a pretty easy-going person. I hardly ever feel stressed. They also say that I am funny - that I make them smile. I am also a loyal friend, and am honest - sometimes to a fault. One friend describes me as gregarious.
In my spare time I look after myself. I like working out at the gym, jogging along the boardwalk near my home, and spending time with my friends and family.

I enjoy life, as you never know what is around the corner. I love doing random things including weekends away exploring and visiting new places. I have been fascinated by different ideas, religions and cultures since I was a child. I love going to see live music, seeing a good comedian, going to the cinema, watching sports and eating out at interesting restaurants.

I have been single for a few years now. This isn't because I'm scared to commit but because I just haven't found that special someone who makes life fall into place. I'm looking for the right person to settle down with. However, I'd rather be a slightly lonely singleton than be with just anyone to be part of a couple, only to quickly break up.

I am not interested in desperate women who want to get married tomorrow. Rome was not built in a day! I have a good job and have been working since my late teens. Someone who can't handle a man with his own goals and aspirations need not respond. The rest is for you to find out, of course. Why not get in touch?
